concepts.text1: Constant-product AMM slippage and impermanent loss
concepts.text9: Deep neural networks estimate the stochastic discount factor (SDF) with the no-arbitrage condition as the objective; large language models (LLMs) are used for economic forecasting and concept measurement.
concepts.text10: Deep SDFs beat traditional linear factor models across Sharpe ratio, explained variance and pricing errors.
concepts.text11: Feed-forward/recurrent networks extract nonlinear factor loadings from hundreds of firm characteristics and train the SDF with GMM moment conditions (pricing-error minimization) as the loss; adversarial networks generate the hardest-to-price portfolios, forcing the SDF to satisfy no-arbitrage.
concepts.text12: SDF weights wᵢ(x) are estimated by a neural network taking characteristics x as input; pricing errors must vanish for every tradeable portfolio's excess return Rᵉ.
concepts.text13: Factor investing, cross-sectional return prediction, asset allocation under macro scenarios; LLMs extract earnings-call/news sentiment as extra state variables.
concepts.text14: Weak black-box interpretability, overfitting, and little robustness to macro structural breaks; out-of-sample decay and data snooping remain the core concerns.
concepts.text16: Bottom-up emergence of macro phenomena from micro individual behavior, with no representative-agent assumption; LLM agents (EconAgent / TradingAgents) reproduce classic macro and trading behavior.
concepts.text17: Multi-agent trader behavior can be aggregated mathematically to derive GARCH volatility clustering; CBDC simulations reveal a reshaping of bank intermediation.
concepts.text18: Define behavioral rules for heterogeneous agents (fundamentalist/trend/noise traders) and iterate them through a market matching mechanism, observing the emergence of macro statistics such as prices and volumes; recently LLMs give agents language-reasoning ability.
concepts.text19: Price adjustment is proportional to the net demand D of fundamentalists versus trend followers, with κ the market depth; nonlinear switching generates fat tails and volatility clustering.
concepts.text20: Stress testing, policy experiments (CBDC, transaction taxes), market-microstructure research, flash-crash and liquidity-drought scenarios.
concepts.text21: Calibration is hard, results are sensitive to behavioral assumptions, and there is no unified falsifiability standard; computational cost rises quickly with the number of agents.
concepts.text24: Financial systems are complex networks (interbank lending, supply chains, trade); graph neural networks (GNNs) extend systemic-risk measurement to graph-structured data.
concepts.text25: Dynamic GNNs capture the time evolution of network structure, quantifying contagion pathways and amplification of systemic risk.
concepts.text26: Model institutions as nodes and exposures as weighted directed edges; message-passing layers aggregate neighbors' risk states, combined with DebtRank / default-contagion models to predict cascading failures and systemically important institutions (SIFIs).
concepts.text27: Node representations h aggregate neighbor information through attention weights αᵢⱼ; multiple propagation layers simulate risk diffusing step by step along the network.
concepts.text28: Central-bank macroprudential oversight, SIFI identification, contagion-path early warning, supply-chain fragility and trade-shock assessment.
concepts.text29: Exposure data are scarce and lagged, network structure is endogenous to the crisis itself, and over-smoothing makes deep GNNs hard to train.
concepts.text34: Integrate physical and transition risk into asset pricing; Climate VaR uses NGFS/IPCC scenarios to assess policy, technology and physical shocks.
concepts.text35: When the carbon tax is below the social cost of carbon, brown assets can act as a hedge — challenging conventional ESG intuition.
concepts.text36: Introduce carbon-price paths and climate scenarios into DCF/asset-pricing frameworks; map physical losses and transition costs into cash-flow shocks, revalue assets under NGFS scenarios and compute tail losses.
concepts.text37: Revalue discounted cash flows for each climate scenario s (orderly/disorderly transition, hot-house world); the quantile loss is Climate VaR.
concepts.text38: ESG portfolio stress testing, sector repricing under transition pathways, green-premium / brown-discount estimation, regulatory climate-scenario disclosure.
concepts.text39: Very high long-horizon scenario uncertainty, no historical data for calibration, and carbon-price and policy-path assumptions driving results.
concepts.text42: Behavioral finance moves from description to quantitative modeling; neuroeconomics feeds brain-imaging data directly into financial decision prediction (MCoRNN-MCD and similar).
concepts.text43: 'Neurofinance' moves from the lab to applications, suggesting decision mechanisms can be measured and modeled directly.
concepts.text44: Overlay physiological/neural signals (fMRI, skin conductance, eye tracking) as state variables on the prospect-theory utility framework, and use deep sequence models to predict risk decisions and shifts in market sentiment.
concepts.text45: Prospect-theory value function: loss-aversion coefficient λ>1 with subjectively weighted probabilities π; neural data estimate individualized α, β, λ.
concepts.text46: Personalized advice, risk-preference measurement, market-sentiment indicators, real-time detection and intervention of behavioral biases.
concepts.text47: Neural data collection is costly with small samples and limited external validity; ethical and privacy constraints limit large-scale use.
concepts.text50: Automated market makers (AMMs) replace order books and liquidity pools replace market makers; DeFi modeling moves from description to rigorous economic analysis.
concepts.text51: Network probability-contagion models quantify systemic-risk propagation over bilateral-liability financial networks.
concepts.text52: Use constant-function market makers (CFMMs) to characterize pool pricing, analyzing impermanent loss, arbitrage and MEV; use network models to study cascading liquidations in lending protocols.
concepts.text53: Constant-product market maker: the product of the two asset reserves in the pool is conserved, with marginal price set by the reserve ratio; large trades create slippage and impermanent loss.
concepts.text54: DEX design, liquidity-mining incentives, liquidation-risk assessment, stablecoins and overcollateralized lending mechanisms.
concepts.text55: Smart-contract risk, oracle manipulation, regulatory uncertainty, and the reflexive fragility of liquidity and liquidations in extreme markets.
concepts.text59: Bring CBDC, banking frictions and multiple policy tools into a unified New Keynesian framework; macroprudential DSGE evaluates the interaction of tools such as LTV/DSTI.
concepts.text60: The effect of CBDC interest-rate policy depends on the monetary anchor regime; with high substitutability a CBDC economy approximates an economy without CBDC.
concepts.text61: Introduce a banking sector, collateral constraints and CBDC as another safe asset into DSGE; evaluate the interaction of macroprudential tools and monetary policy through impulse responses and welfare analysis.
concepts.text62: Collateral constraint: the borrowing cap is proportional to the loan-to-value ratio θ and expected future collateral value; LTV/DSTI tools damp procyclical leverage by adjusting θ.
concepts.text63: Central-bank digital currency design, macroprudential policy mixes, bank-disintermediation risk, interest-rate transmission analysis.
concepts.text64: Linear solution methods miss crisis nonlinearities, behavioral foundations face the Lucas critique, and parameters drive welfare conclusions.
concepts.ui.text2: AI/ML · agent-based simulation · complex networks · climate finance · neuroeconomics · DeFi · macrofinance — a concept map (tracking the latest literature)

zerobeta.chartHint: Black (1972): when risk-free borrowing is unavailable, the zero-beta return E(Rz) replaces Rf. Since E(Rz)>Rf the SML intercept rises and its slope flattens — exactly the empirical pattern of high low-β returns and low high-β returns.
zerobeta.n1: Relaxes the risk-free asset assumption. The zero-beta portfolio is the minimum-variance portfolio uncorrelated with the market.
zerobeta.n2: Rf is replaced by E(Rz), typically with E(Rz)>Rf.
zerobeta.n3: Explains the flatter-than-theory SML documented by Black-Jensen-Scholes (1972).

duality.n1: m = E[m] − b'(f − E f), with b = Σ_f⁻¹ λ / E[m].
duality.n2: So “finding factors” and “finding the pricing kernel” are the same exercise: APT / Fama-French regressions restrict m to the span of the factors.

hjdist.chart2: Pricing errors α across test portfolios
hjdist.chart2Hint: A monotone spread of positive and negative α means the model omits a systematic factor aligned with that sort.
hjdist.n1: Workflow: run time-series regressions for α → weight by the second-moment matrix E[RR′] → δ = √(α′E[RR′]⁻¹α). Smaller δ means the candidate SDF prices all test assets more accurately.
hjdist.n2: δ vs GRS: GRS is a statistical test (is α significantly nonzero?), the HJ distance is an economic measure (how much money is mispriced?). With long samples GRS rejects almost surely, while δ stays comparable.

dynamic.note2a: Once the risk premium is predictable (mean-reverting), the optimal solution gains an

explain.wwr: Wrong-way risk: when default intensity λ_C is positively correlated with the interest rate r, defaults are more likely to occur at times of large exposure → CVA is significantly amplified.
explain.bcva: BCVA = CVA − DVA (Hull-White 2012): the bank's own default losses that are not paid out offset part of the CVA.

explain.vasicekFormula: X_i = √ρ·M + √(1−ρ)·ε_i, default occurs when X_i ≤ Φ⁻¹(PD).
explain.tCopula: The t-Copula introduces a common scale factor W ~ χ²_df/df, producing strong tail dependence → extreme joint default probabilities rise significantly, a key driver of the excess losses in the 2008 crisis.
explain.baselIrb: The Basel II IRB formula is derived from the Vasicek large-portfolio limit: K = LGD·[Φ((Φ⁻¹(PD)+√ρ·Φ⁻¹(0.999))/√(1−ρ)) − PD].

behavior.title: Behavioral Finance Lab
behavior.subtitle: From prospect theory and myopic loss aversion to the BSV / DHS / Hong-Stein belief models, limits to arbitrage, investor sentiment and behavioral corporate finance — eight interactive experiments turning bounded rationality into reproducible price paths.

cpt.title: Cumulative Prospect Theory: value function, probability weighting and the fourfold pattern
cpt.desc: v(x) is defined relative to a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper on the loss side (λ>1); w(p) overweights small and underweights moderate-to-high probabilities. Together they produce the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes, explaining why lotteries and insurance coexist.

note.label: Limitations:
note.text: The reference point r is neither directly observable nor exogenous; different reference points yield very different predictions. Attributing every reluctance to cut losses to loss aversion ignores rational explanations such as taxes, trading costs, private information and learning.

mla.title: Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium puzzle
mla.desc: Benartzi-Thaler: combining loss aversion λ with evaluation frequency endogenously produces a high required return on equities. The more often you evaluate, the more likely you see a loss and the higher the psychological cost — a behavioral explanation of the equity premium puzzle.

chart.utility: Prospect utility vs premium (zero crossing = equilibrium premium)

note.label: Debate:
note.text: Evaluation frequency is unobservable and long-horizon investors need not settle daily; whether differences in evaluation periods between institutions and retail investors actually map into prices remains disputed.

bsv.title: BSV: conservatism + representativeness → underreaction then overreaction
bsv.desc: Investors believe earnings switch between a mean-reverting and a trending regime. Conservatism causes underreaction at announcement followed by slow drift; representativeness extrapolates streaks of good news, pushing prices past fundamentals before a long-run reversal.

chart.car: Post-event cumulative abnormal return (CAR) vs rational baseline

note.label: Testing:
note.text: BSV's falsifiable implication is cross-sectional — drift and reversal should be stronger for stocks with vaguer information and less analyst coverage. That is what separates it from risk-premium explanations.

dhs.title: DHS: overconfidence and self-attribution bias
dhs.desc: Investors overestimate private-signal precision (k>1), causing immediate overreaction; self-attribution lets confirming public news further strengthen beliefs (continued momentum), until public information eventually pulls prices back to fundamentals — long-run reversal.

hs.title: Slow information diffusion + momentum traders: a unified explanation
hs.desc: News diffuses gradually to news-watchers over z periods, creating natural underreaction; momentum traders follow the past j-period trend, amplifying underreaction into overshoot and eventual reversal. No individual-level cognitive bias is required.

chart.price: Price path under slow diffusion + trend chasing

limits.title: Limits to arbitrage: margins, redemptions and forced liquidation
limits.desc: Shleifer-Vishny: spotting a mispricing is not the same as correcting it. Noise-trader risk first widens the mispricing, paper losses trigger redemptions that erode capital, and margins squeeze positions further — so mispricing can persist over economically meaningful horizons.

chart.mis: Mispricing path: constrained vs frictionless arbitrage

note.head: Heterogeneity test:
note.body: The key to a credible behavioral explanation is that the effect is stronger where arbitrage is harder (high short-sale costs, poor substitutes, low institutional ownership); otherwise a risk-premium explanation is hard to rule out.

sentiment.title: Investor sentiment and the cross-section of returns
sentiment.desc: When sentiment is high, hard-to-value, hard-to-arbitrage stocks (small, young, unprofitable, volatile, extreme growth) get bid up and later earn lower returns; the reverse holds when sentiment is low. Sentiment does not price risk, but it determines whose mispricing survives.

note.head: Measurement issue:
note.body: Each sentiment proxy (closed-end fund discount, IPO first-day returns, turnover, consumer confidence) is noisy and endogenous; the robust approach is cross-validating several proxies rather than relying on a single index.

corporate.title: Managerial overconfidence and market timing
corporate.desc: A two-way framework: on one side, "irrational managers + rational markets" — overconfident CEOs believe external finance is undervalued, so investment is highly sensitive to internal cash flow and takeover premiums are too high; on the other, "rational managers + irrational markets" — managers time equity issues, making capital structure the cumulative outcome of past valuations.

chart.timing: Market timing: equity issuance and leverage dynamics

note.head: Identification challenge:
note.body: Investment–cash flow sensitivity can also be explained by financing constraints; overconfidence proxies (late option exercise, insider buying, press wording) may capture private information rather than bias. Credible designs need exogenous shocks or institutional changes.

header.heading: Macro Frontier Lab
header.intro:
Filling four gaps in the macro spectrum: endogenous growth and growth accounting, cyclical mechanisms and the microfoundations of nominal rigidity, policy rules and fiscal–monetary coordination,
          open-economy parity, and contemporary frontiers (behavioral macro, unconventional policy, macrofinance, climate). This complements the classic models of /s/macro and the
          debt/FX/BGG/ZLB experiments of /s/macro-lab.

misc.k15: The residual captures both genuine technological progress and factor utilization, allocative efficiency, and measurement error — the source of the "TFP is a measure of our ignorance" critique.

misc.k33: A typical finding: more than half of cross-country income gaps come from efficiency/TFP rather than factor accumulation — shifting attention toward institutions, allocative efficiency, and technology diffusion.

misc.k50: Endogenous cycles require no exogenous shock: the accelerator ties investment to changes in output, and the roots of c·v determine oscillation and convergence/divergence.
misc.k57: At the ZLB / monetary policy does not offset
misc.k68: The red line marks 1: whether the multiplier exceeds 1 depends on slack, whether monetary policy offsets it, and households' degree of Ricardian equivalence — not a fixed constant.
misc.k82:
RBC's contribution is methodological (stochastic dynamic general equilibrium + calibration + moment matching); its controversy lies in explaining recessions as technological regress, requiring high Frisch elasticities,
            and lacking monetary and financial frictions.
misc.k90: Probability of no price change θ
misc.k102: θ → κ and Price Duration Mapping
misc.k119: Without a commitment mechanism, the public anticipates the central bank's expansionary motive → inflation is higher but output is unchanged. Central bank independence, inflation targeting, and conservative central bankers are all commitment technologies.
misc.k120: Performance of Four Policy Rules under a Cost-Push Shock
misc.k135: Price-level targeting gains an extra expectations channel by "making up for" past deviations, so cumulative drift is smaller — at the cost of potentially larger short-run output volatility.
misc.k157: Fama Regression: Δs vs. Interest Rate Differential Scatter
misc.k161:
UIP predicts β=1; empirically one often gets β<0: high-interest currencies not only fail to depreciate but deliver positive carry returns. Risk premia, tail risk, and
            limited arbitrage capital are candidate explanations. The CIP basis has stayed persistently nonzero since 2008, showing that even "riskless" parity is constrained by balance sheets.
misc.k183: Adjustment Path after a Sudden Stop
misc.k188:
Under currency mismatch, depreciation brings both expenditure switching (expansionary) and balance-sheet losses (contractionary); when the latter dominates, depreciation becomes contractionary — the core motive behind
            "original sin" and FX reserve self-insurance.
misc.k200:
The FIRE benchmark requires forecast errors to be unpredictable. Sticky information yields a positive CG coefficient (underreaction), diagnostic expectations a negative one (overreaction),
            and adaptive learning produces systematic catch-up after shocks — these three deviations are exactly behavioral macro's empirical handles.
misc.k233: QE lowers the term premium via portfolio rebalancing and the expected short-rate path via signaling; YCC replaces a quantity target with a price commitment, and purchases can actually be smaller when credible.
misc.k256: Net worth loss × target leverage = the scale of asset contraction; the fire-sale price impact turns individually prudent behavior into systemic tightening — the target of macroprudential policy.
misc.k277: Emissions Path and Output Cost Decomposition
misc.k284:
Carbon pricing internalizes the externality, showing up short-term as a supply-side cost and "green inflation," in exchange for lower physical damage long-term.
            A disorderly transition (late and abrupt) raises both transition costs and financial risk — the core scenario contrast in central bank climate stress tests.

fiV62.s43: Markets directly observe par yields on coupon bonds, while pricing requires discount factors. Bootstrapping strips out coupons sequentially from short to long maturities, translating the par curve into a zero-coupon curve and an instantaneous forward curve: an upward-sloping par curve necessarily implies a steeper zero curve, and the forward curve is steeper still.
fiV62.s56: Interpolation is not a harmless technical detail: the same set of nodes can produce radically different forward curves under different methods. Linear interpolation of zero rates creates jumps in forwards at the nodes; piecewise-constant forwards produce a step function; splines are smoothest but may oscillate. Forward-curve roughness (the sum of squared second differences) is a standard diagnostic for choosing an interpolation method.
fiV62.s66: If the curve is completely unchanged one year from now, a bond’s holding-period return comes from two sources: carry (coupon/yield less financing cost) and roll-down (capital gain as the bond rolls down the curve toward shorter maturities). The steeper the curve, the greater the roll-down. This is the source of returns for curve trades and carry portfolios—and their greatest vulnerability when the curve flattens.
fiV62.s74: Four Spread Measures: Nominal / Z / ASW / OAS
fiV62.s75: The four spread measures answer four different questions: the nominal spread is measured against a single benchmark point; the Z-spread against the entire curve; ASW quotes the bond against the swap curve after converting it to floating-rate cash flows; and OAS goes one step further by stripping out the embedded option. The identity Z − OAS = option cost is the first check that an option-embedded bond is priced correctly.
fiV62.s84: Analytical duration applies only to option-free fixed cash flows. A bond with embedded options has cash flows that change with interest rates, so the correct approach is to reprice after shifting the entire curve up and down: effective duration =(P₋−P₊)/(2P₀Δy), effective convexity =(P₊+P₋−2P₀)/(P₀Δy²). A callable bond has negative convexity at low rates because its price is capped by the call price.
fiV62.s92: A parallel shift is only one dimension of curve risk. Key rate duration decomposes total duration across maturity buckets; hedging requires a set of benchmark bonds to neutralize each bucket separately. This is also the technical prerequisite for expressing a standalone view on curve steepening or flattening.
fiV62.s103: The goal of liability-driven investing is not to maximize returns, but to immunize surplus against interest rates. The Redington conditions require matching dollar duration and asset convexity greater than liability convexity: surplus is then first-order insensitive to small parallel shifts and positive to second order. Once the gap turns positive, a rise in rates directly erodes capital.
fiV62.s116: An embedded option bends a bond’s price-yield curve: the issuer owns the call, which caps the price near the call price at the low-rate end (negative convexity); the investor owns the put, which provides downside protection at the high-rate end. Option value = option-free bond value minus option-embedded bond value, and increases monotonically with interest-rate volatility.
fiV62.s125: Convertible Bond Decomposition: Bond Floor + Conversion Option
fiV62.s126: A convertible bond = bond floor + equity call option. At low share prices, the bond floor dominates and it behaves like a credit bond; at high share prices, conversion parity dominates and delta approaches the conversion ratio; in between is a hybrid region, priced by both volatility and credit spread. The conversion premium measures how much extra you pay for optionality.
fiV62.s143: Credit Spread Decomposition & the Credit Spread Puzzle
fiV62.s144: Investment-grade bond spreads are far higher than historical default losses can explain—this is the credit spread puzzle. Decomposing observed spreads into expected loss, compensation for bearing default risk, liquidity premium and tax effects typically still leaves a substantial residual, pointing to pricing factors beyond the model.
fiV62.s157: Credit risk is not just default: a downgrade alone can cause losses through spread repricing. Raising a one-year transition matrix to successive powers gives multi-period distributions; cumulative default probability rises convexly with horizon. Converting each state’s spread change into a loss and taking the quantile gives CreditMetrics-style migration-risk VaR.
fiV62.s169: Risk allocation in structured products is encoded in the cash-flow waterfall: principal is repaid in order of seniority, while losses are absorbed from the bottom up. Once an overcollateralization trigger is breached, interest is diverted to repay senior principal—this is how mezzanine holders can suddenly see cash flows dry up in a crisis.
fiV62.s187: Correlation does not change the pool’s expected loss; it changes how losses are allocated across tranches. As correlation rises, the probabilities of both widespread defaults and no defaults rise; the equity tranche can benefit, while the senior tranche is significantly impaired. This is the source of the correlation smile and the pricing rationale behind “even AAA can break” in 2007.
fiV62.s196: There are two ways to express exposure to the same credit: buy the cash bond and finance it, or sell protection. In theory, the spreads should be equal; in practice, financing costs, repo specialness and balance-sheet constraints drive a basis wedge. A negative basis means the cash bond is cheap, but capturing it requires reliable ongoing financing—financing was precisely what broke first in 2008.
fiV62.s212: Mortgage borrowers hold a free refinancing option. When rates fall, prepayments accelerate and MBS duration shortens; investors are forced to reinvest at lower rates. When rates rise, prepayments dry up and duration extends. This “heads you lose, tails you lose” duration drift is negative convexity and the reason hedges must be continually rebalanced.
fiV62.s220: Repo allows a fixed-income portfolio to support a large asset base with little equity: leverage amplifies both carry and duration risk, and it can take only a few dozen basis points to reach the breaking point. When haircuts rise under market stress, forced selling depresses prices; falling prices then erode equity further—this is the funding-liquidity spiral of Brunnermeier-Pedersen.
fiV62.s232: LIBOR is a forward-looking fixing, while risk-free rates such as SOFR are overnight rates compounded in arrears: at the start of the period, the interest amount is unknown. Compounding has a positive convexity benefit relative to a simple average; converting legacy contracts requires an ISDA-style historical median fallback spread. Negative rates invalidate the lognormal assumption, while the shifted-lognormal model shifts the forward rate and strike together back into positive territory.
fiV62.s247: Two pricing factors are difficult to capture in traditional models. First, climate: the green label can command a demand-driven negative premium, while carbon exposure requires compensation for transition risk. Second, liquidity: corporate bonds trade infrequently, so bid-ask spreads must be amortized over the holding period, with additional compensation for search costs and Amihud-style price impact.

microV61.k040: A market maker is a two-sided queueing system: quotes determine arrival rates on both sides, while inventory and cash each drift; whenever buy and sell flows are imbalanced, bankruptcy (depletion of inventory or cash) is almost certain within finite time.
microV61.k058: Quoted spread = order-processing cost + inventory-carrying cost + adverse-selection cost. The first two are temporary (prices revert, producing Roll-type negative autocovariance); adverse selection is permanent (the midpoint is genuinely revised).
microV61.k067: Rather than quoting symmetrically around the midpoint, a market maker quotes around the reservation price r = S − q·γσ²(T−t): more inventory shifts quotes downward overall to attract buying and discourage selling. Spread width is jointly determined by risk aversion and order-flow intensity k.
microV61.k082: Daily buy and sell counts are generated by a three-state mixed Poisson process: no news / good news / bad news. The log-likelihood (stabilized with log-sum-exp) is used to infer α, δ, μ, ε, yielding PIN = αμ / (αμ + ε_b + ε_s).
microV61.k094: Bin trades into equal-volume buckets (volume clock), approximate buy/sell shares using bulk classification, and calculate |V_buy − V_sell| / V on a rolling basis. Inject one-sided toxic flow midway through and observe how VPIN rises before prices collapse.
microV61.k105: Make-or-Take: the option value of limit orders
microV61.k106: Posting a limit order is equivalent to selling a free trading option: if executed, it earns the half-spread and a rebate, but execution often occurs in an adverse direction (adverse selection); if unfilled, it incurs the opportunity cost of alpha decay. Queue position determines the probability of execution.
microV61.k121: A Farmer-Patelli-Zovko-style three-Poisson-flow model: limit orders, market orders, and cancellations are all random. Even without any strategic behavior, statistical patterns in spreads and depth emerge (spreads rise with market-order flow; depth accumulates with limit-order flow)—market structure itself explains a substantial share of liquidity.
microV61.k133: Trades trigger trades: λ(t) = μ + Σ α e^{−β(t−t_i)}. The branching ratio n = α/β measures endogeneity—when n approaches 1, the market is almost entirely self-driven, explaining flash crashes and trade clustering.
microV61.k148: Spread measures, high-low estimators, and trade-direction classification
microV61.k149: Effective spread = realized spread + price impact: the former is the compensation actually captured by market makers, while the latter is what information takes away. Without tick data, use Corwin-Schultz high-low estimation; without quotes, classify direction using the tick / Lee-Ready rule—misclassification systematically attenuates all measures.
microV61.k158: Square-root impact law and permanent/temporary decomposition
microV61.k159: A robust empirical regularity across markets and asset classes: ΔP/P ≈ Y·σ·(Q/V)^δ, δ ≈ 0.5. Concavity means order splitting is effective but with diminishing marginal benefit; only the permanent component reflects information, while the temporary component reverts over time—the portion execution algorithms can genuinely save.
microV61.k174: Price discovery: Hasbrouck information shares and Gonzalo-Granger weights
microV61.k175: When the same asset trades on two markets, which one leads? The VECM error-correction loadings determine common-factor weights (GG), while Cholesky orderings of the innovation covariance yield lower and upper bounds on information shares (IS). The higher the correlation, the wider the bounds and the less identifiable the conclusion.
microV61.k188: Mechanism effects of the minimum price increment (Tick Size)
microV61.k189: When the tick exceeds the frictionless spread, the spread is artificially elevated, price priority ceases to matter and time priority dominates; market makers earn queue rents and depth accumulates. A tick that is too small makes spreads more responsive but depth thin, while quote jumping proliferates—this is the core trade-off of the SEC Tick Size Pilot.
microV61.k201: Batch matching pools dispersed noise into a single price, with pricing error falling as √batch size. This explains opening/closing auctions, auctions for illiquid instruments, and frequent batch auctions (FBA) as a market-design proposal to counter latency arbitrage.
microV61.k211: Circuit breakers give the market time to reaggregate liquidity (the cooling-off effect), but may also create a magnet effect: as prices approach the threshold, traders rush to execute first, accelerating the trigger. The threshold, halt duration, and cooling strength jointly determine the net effect.
microV61.k222: Dark pools execute at the midpoint but offer no execution certainty, attracting uninformed flow that is insensitive to execution speed. A higher proportion of informed flow is therefore left on displayed markets, increasing adverse selection, widening spreads, and thinning depth—the theoretical basis for regulatory caps on dark-pool market share.
microV61.k232: The third dimension of liquidity is neither spread nor depth, but resilience: how quickly liquidity recovers after a shock. Market-maker withdrawal causes depth to collapse, which in turn widens spreads, creating a feedback spiral—beyond a critical threshold, liquidity no longer returns; it disappears.
microV61.k244: Amihud-Mendelson liquidity premium and holding-period clienteles
microV61.k245: Trading costs are amortized over the holding period: short-horizon clienteles can hold only low-spread assets, while long-horizon clienteles are willing to hold high-spread assets and demand compensation. The equilibrium relationship between spreads and expected gross returns is concave—this is how microstructure costs enter asset pricing.

puzzles.text21: How EIS pins down both the premium and the interest rate
puzzles.text22: Separating γ and ψ lets γ control the risk premium and ψ control the risk-free rate. With ψ>1, flexible intertemporal substitution means long-run risk lowers rather than raises Rf—the key to resolving both puzzles together.
puzzles.text24: m = θ·lnδ − (θ/ψ)Δc + (θ−1)r_c; shock loadings imply λ_η = γ and λ_e = (1−θ)κ₁A₁φₑ.
puzzles.text25: When ψ = 1/γ, θ = 1 and the long-run risk price vanishes, reducing the model to power-utility CCAPM. Persistence of growth, not consumption risk alone, is central to the puzzle.
puzzles.text37: Can be high even with small γ
puzzles.text43: Surplus consumption ratio S vs. effective risk aversion / Sharpe
puzzles.text44: As consumption approaches habit, S falls sharply and effective risk aversion γ/S surges. The same investors demand much more compensation in recessions, generating predictability and excess volatility.
puzzles.text47: External habit X_t slowly follows past consumption; S = (C−X)/C. Utility curvature stays moderate (γ≈2), but effective risk aversion γ/S increases manyfold in bad times.
puzzles.text48: CC designs the sensitivity function λ(s) to keep the risk-free rate constant, explaining the high equity premium without creating a risk-free rate puzzle.
puzzles.text56: Consumption drop in a disaster b (%)
puzzles.text65: How disaster size b affects both premiums and interest rates
puzzles.text66: Disasters raise the equity premium and lower the risk-free rate, addressing two puzzles with one parameter. Such events are rarely observed in sample, so identification relies on long international histories (Barro's 20th-century disaster sample).
puzzles.text70: Ordinary diffusion risk contributes very little; most of the premium comes from surging marginal utility in the tail branch (1−b)^{−γ}.
puzzles.text71: / [(1−p) + p(1−b)^(−γ)]: the disaster branch raises E[m], lowering the risk-free rate.
puzzles.text72: Criticism: results are highly sensitive to the tail shape of b and hard to reconcile with option-implied disaster insurance prices (Backus-Chernov-Martin).
puzzles.text73: Premium too low, Rf too high: raising γ also pushes Rf into double digits (the risk-free rate puzzle).
puzzles.text75: ψ>1 separates risk aversion from substitution, matching high premiums and low rates; it relies on a persistent component that is difficult to test directly.
puzzles.text77: Time-varying effective risk aversion naturally explains predictability and excess volatility; results are sensitive to S dynamics.
puzzles.text79: One tail parameter raises premiums and lowers rates; identification relies on international disaster histories outside the sample.
puzzles.text91: Three criteria: a sufficiently high premium, a sufficiently low rate, and σ(m)/E(m) above the Hansen-Jagannathan bound (historical maximum Sharpe ≈ 0.4).
puzzles.text95: The three puzzles are facets of one constraint: the pricing kernel must be volatile enough (equity premium), have a sufficiently high mean (risk-free rate), and exhibit state-dependent volatility (excess volatility and predictability).
puzzles.text96: No single approach wins. Current models combine long-run risk, time-varying risk aversion, and tail risk in one SDF, jointly identified using options, bonds, and cross-sectional data.

frontier.text21: Long-horizon return regressions: coefficients, R², and Hodrick t statistics
frontier.text22: β and R² increase with the horizon, largely due to mechanically overlapping observations. Hodrick (1992) standard errors account for overlap and usually reduce t statistics substantially.
frontier.text26: High dp (cheap prices relative to dividends) predicts higher subsequent returns—direct evidence of time-varying discount rates.
frontier.text28: Discount-rate news explains most US dp variation: stock-price volatility mainly reflects changing risk premiums rather than revised cash-flow expectations (the modern view of Shiller's excess-volatility puzzle).
frontier.text29: Log-linear identity: dp_t ≈ Σ ρ^j (r_(t+1+j) − Δd_(t+1+j)). Cheap prices relative to dividends imply higher future returns or weaker future dividends.
frontier.text30: Unpredictable returns and predictable dividends cannot both hold: Cochrane's b_r − b_d + ρφ = 1 expresses this restriction in regression form.
frontier.text51: Principal-component decomposition: nominal factors ≫ effective dimension
frontier.text52: With high commonality, the first 2–3 components explain most variance: hundreds of factors contain far fewer independent signals.
frontier.text58: Harvey-Liu-Zhu (2016): hundreds of papers search the same data for factors, invalidating the usual t>2 threshold; use |t| > 3.
frontier.text59: Ridge handles collinearity by spreading coefficients across correlated factors; LASSO selects by shrinking noise factors to zero. Neither replaces economic theory—selected does not mean priced.
frontier.text65: Fama slope β (depreciation response to rate differential)
frontier.text72: Fama (1984) regression: rate differential vs. realized depreciation
frontier.text73: UIP predicts a 45° line (β=1), with depreciation offsetting the rate differential. Data often show β<1 or even negative: high-yield currencies can appreciate, generating systematic carry profits.
frontier.text76: Carry returns sorted by rate differential
frontier.text77: Sort on forward discounts: buy high-yield and sell low-yield currencies. The flip side is crash risk—carry loses during global risk aversion and is highly exposed to bad states.
frontier.text80: In complete markets, Δs = ln m* − ln m: FX changes equal the difference between national pricing kernels. Carry premiums thus reflect asymmetric SDF volatility, with lower volatility in high-rate countries.
frontier.text81: Explanations include crash and disaster exposure (Brunnermeier-Nagel-Pedersen), the global dollar factor (Lustig-Roussanov-Verdelhan), and incomplete-market gaps in international risk sharing.

sdf.text21: Pricing kernel M vs. market return
sdf.text22: M is high in bad times (market crashes). Assets positively correlated with bad times (high cov(M,R)) have low risk and premiums; hedging assets (negative ρ) can require negative premiums.
sdf.text24: Beta representation: E[Ri]−Rf = −(1+Rf)·cov(M,Ri). Closer model and input premiums indicate more accurate pricing by this linear SDF.
sdf.text28: Every asset-pricing model can be written as p = E[M·X], where M is the stochastic discount factor / pricing kernel.
sdf.text30: E[Ri]−Rf = −Rf·cov(M,Ri) = −(1+Rf)·cov(M,Ri). Assets positively correlated with bad times (high M) have low risk.
sdf.text32: M = a − b·Rm implies CAPM; M = δ(C′/C)^(−γ) implies CCAPM. These are different specifications of M.
sdf.text55: Equity premium vs. risk aversion γ
sdf.text56: The standard consumption model produces tiny premiums for plausible γ (2–4). Matching the historical 6% needs γ≈50: the Mehra-Prescott (1985) equity premium puzzle.
sdf.text60: Risk premium = covariance of returns and consumption growth × risk aversion; M = δ(C′/C)^(−γ).
sdf.text62: Consumption is too smooth (σc≈3.6%) for standard γ to explain the historical 6% premium.
sdf.text64: Raising γ to match the premium also raises the model risk-free rate, contradicting the observed ~1%.
sdf.text81: The gold line is the HJ bound σ(M) = Sharpe·E(M). Every valid pricing kernel must lie above it (shaded region). The red point is calibrated CCAPM σ(M); below the bound, consumption volatility cannot explain the high Sharpe.
sdf.text88: Any valid pricing kernel needs enough volatility to match the observed Sharpe, imposing a lower bound on M.
sdf.text90: Standard consumption SDF volatility σ(M)≈γσc is too small to reach the bound unless γ is enormous.

macroTheory.title: Macroeconomics Reading Guide: From Growth and Fluctuations to Policy, Open Economy, and Frontiers
macroTheory.subtitle: Macroeconomics is not simply "aggregated microeconomics." Even when every household and firm makes rational choices, the economy as a whole can still fall into insufficient demand, persistent unemployment, financial panic, or runaway inflation. It truly addresses aggregate outcomes, coordination problems, and systemic fluctuations.
macroTheory.mainLine: A central theme: In the long run, macroeconomics explains why productive capacity grows; in the short run, it explains why actual output deviates from potential output; at the policy level, it discusses whether and how monetary, fiscal, and institutional arrangements can and should reduce these deviations, balancing efficiency, stability, distribution, and risk.

tfp.title: TFP IS A "MEASURE OF IGNORANCE"
tfp.content: The residual absorbs technological progress, factor utilization, allocative efficiency, and measurement error simultaneously. The debate over whether East Asian growth is input-driven or efficiency-driven (Krugman-Young vs. subsequent research) remains unresolved precisely because the residual itself depends on share assumptions and factor quality adjustments.

forwardGuidance.title: THE FORWARD GUIDANCE PUZZLE
forwardGuidance.content: In standard NK models, interest rate commitments further into the future have a larger impact on today, with a magnitude significantly exceeding empirical findings. This is a signal of the model's over-reliance on assumptions of perfect rationality and perfect information, leading to the introduction of sticky information, bounded rationality, and heterogeneous agents.

devaluation.title: DEVALUATION IS NOT ALWAYS EXPANSIONARY
devaluation.content: When currency mismatches exist (foreign currency liabilities, local currency assets), devaluation brings both expenditure switching (expansionary) and balance sheet losses (contractionary). When the latter dominates, devaluation is contractionary—this is the core logic of the emerging market "original sin" and reserve self-insurance.

postPandemic.title: CHALLENGES OF THE POST-PANDEMIC AND HIGH INFLATION ERA
postPandemic.content: Inflation from 2021–2023 was neither purely demand-driven nor purely supply-driven: fiscal transfers, supply chain disruptions, changes in labor supply, and expectations all played a role. It exposed two risks: over-reliance on the supply-side judgment that "inflation is transitory," and ignoring the impact of fiscal-monetary interaction on the price level.

judgmentRules.title: THREE RULES FOR MACRO JUDGMENT
judgmentRules.content: 1. Ask whether the shock comes from demand or supply before asking about policy; 2. Any "multiplier" or "transmission coefficient" is a state-dependent parameter, not a constant; 3. Maintain a falsifiable attitude toward models: DSGE, HANK, and narrative analysis each have blind spots, and cross-validation is more robust than betting on a single framework.

ols.down: OLS β̂={{ols}} sits below the true β={{b}} (bias {{bias}}); IV β̂={{iv}} is closer to the truth.
ols.weak: Weak instrument: IV β̂={{iv}} is unstable with large variance while OLS β̂={{ols}} has bias {{bias}} — weak IV is not automatically better.
